source: Julius Caesar at the Rubicon, 49 BC (Suetonius, Divus Iulius 32)
note: Probably said in Greek, quoting the comic poet Menander: ἀνερρίφθω κύβος.

english: I came, I saw, I conquered.
source: Caesar's dispatch after Zela, 47 BC (Suetonius, Divus Iulius 37)
note: Three words, one campaign. Peak efficiency.

source: Cato the Elder, ending every speech (Plutarch, Cato Maior 27)
note: Status: completed, 146 BC.

english: The Senate and People of Rome.
source: SPQR — on standards, coins and inscriptions
note: Still on Rome's manhole covers. The Senate and the People have mostly changed.
Agile methodology, first century BC.

source: Augustus's reported last words (Suetonius, Divus Augustus 99)
note: Exit, stage left, after forty-one years.

english: What an artist dies in me!
note: Reviews were mixed.

source: Brennus, at the Gallic sack of Rome, c. 390 BC (Livy 5.48)
note: Said while throwing his sword on the scales to raise the ransom.

source: Vespasian, on the urine tax (Suetonius, Vespasian 23)
note: Public urinals in Italy are still sometimes called vespasiani.
Suetonius has Caesar say "καὶ σύ, τέκνον;" — "You too, child?" — in Greek, if he said anything at all.

source: Traditionally whispered to triumphing generals (cf. Tertullian, Apologeticus 33)
note: The phrasing is later; the idea is Roman.
Juvenal was complaining, not recommending.

english: If you want peace, prepare for war.
source: After Vegetius, De Re Militari 3 (4th–5th century)
note: Vegetius actually wrote "qui desiderat pacem, praeparet bellum". Also the origin of "Parabellum".
Now the motto of South Carolina and of the University of St Andrews.

source: Cicero, Pro Roscio Amerino 84, crediting the judge Lucius Cassius
note: Still the first question in every investigation.

english: Oh the times, oh the customs!
note: Every generation, forever.

latin: Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?
english: How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?
note: The most famous opening line in Latin oratory. Catiline left town that night.
Full line: carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero — seize the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow.
The shortest complete breakdown in Latin literature.

english: I sing of arms and the man.
note: The Empire's founding epic, commissioned by management.

latin: Tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento.
english: Remember, Roman, to rule the peoples with your power.
note: Anchises's job description for Rome. The contract has lapsed.

english: They make a desert and call it peace.
note: The Empire, reviewed by a customer.
Tacitus's stated method. Results varied.

english: Who will guard the guards themselves?
note: Originally about chaperones. Now about everything.

latin: Quidquid id est, timeo Danaos et dona ferentes.
english: Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts.
note: Laocoön, regarding a certain horse.
Correct, as it turns out.

english: I have built a monument more lasting than bronze.
note: The poems outlasted the bronze — and the Empire.

latin: Aequam memento rebus in arduis servare mentem.
english: Remember to keep a level head in hard times.
note: Imperial Stoicism for busy people.

english: A sound mind in a sound body.
note: Juvenal's suggestion for what you should actually be praying for.

english: I have granted them empire without end.
note: Terms and conditions applied. See: 476, 1453.
Also this site's operating principle: one check a day, indefinitely.
Roman parents used it to frighten children. It mostly worked.

source: Tibullus 2.5.23; coin legends from Hadrian onwards
note: The city, yes. The Empire, see above.

english: Thus passes the glory of the world.
source: Medieval (papal coronation rite, after Thomas à Kempis) — not classical
note: Not Roman, but it is about Rome in spirit, so it stays.

english: Caesar is not above the grammarians.
source: Proverbial since the Council of Constance (1414); the idea goes back to Suetonius, De Grammaticis 22
note: Tiberius, corrected on a word: "You can give citizenship to men, Caesar, but not to words."
